newsitem.title: UKRAINE: IMF money would support Ukraine currency corridor.
newsitem.headline: IMF money would support Ukraine currency corridor.

text.p: International Monetary Fund (IMF) approval of long-term funding for Ukraine would help the country implement a currency corridor for the hryvnia, the president's economic adviser said.

Ukraine is awaiting approval of a three-year, $2.5-3.0 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) from the IMF, but this depends largely on passage of a tough budget through parliament early in the new year.
"It (the EFF) would allow the National Bank of Ukraine to implement a currency corridor," Valery Lytvytsky told reporters on Wednesday.
He said the central bank did not have enough reserves -- estimated at about $2 billion -- to support a corridor.
The country has been discussing a new currency regime since the hryvnia was introduced in September to replace the interim karbovanets currency.

Lytvytsky said the IMF money could be used as a hryvnia "stabilisation fund", after Ukraine dropped a request for a specific $1.5 billion currency stabilisation fund from the IMF because there were too many conditions attached to it.
The presidential adviser said Ukraine could next year receive up to $1.07 billion of the EFF, which will succeed the $867 million stand-by programme approved in May.
He said Ukraine expected to receive $3.424 billion in foreign aid in 1997, compared to $2.385 billion this year.

The funds would include $1 billion from the World Bank, $300 million from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), $554 million from the U.S., $220 million from Germany, $35 million from Japan and $125 million from the European Union, plus other credits, he said.
The requested increase in foreign funding would help the authorities solve Ukraine's wage payment crisis, create conditions for economic growth and pay off some debts, Lytvystky said.
None of Ukraine's donors objected to a currency corridor for the hryvnia, he added.

Western donors said at a Washington meeting this month that they were prepared to give Ukraine more than $5 billion in the next three years if it demonstrated continued success with its economic reform programme, started in 1994.
Ukraine planned to pay Russia $1 billion next year for energy debts accumulated from 1992-95, Lytvystsky added.
The wage debt, owed to teachers, doctors, miners and government workers, stands at about $1.6 billion.
